cards.b: The process by which plants synthesise carbohydrates from raw materials using energy from light.

cards.f: Word equation and balanced equation for photosynthesis
cards.b: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (light, chlorophyll). 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
Green pigment in chloroplasts; transfers energy from light into energy in chemicals for making carbohydrates.

cards.f: Uses of carbohydrates made in photosynthesis
cards.b: Starch: energy store. Cellulose: cell walls. Glucose: respiration. Sucrose: transport in phloem. Nectar: attracts pollinators.

cards.f: Why do plants need nitrate and magnesium ions?
cards.b: Nitrate: to make amino acids (proteins). Magnesium: to make chlorophyll.

cards.f: How do you read a limiting factor graph?
cards.b: Where the line rises, the factor on the x-axis is limiting. Where it levels off, another factor (CO₂, temperature, light) is limiting.
Yellow: more CO₂ than air. Orange/red: same as air. Purple: less CO₂ than air (photosynthesis faster than respiration).

cards.f: Steps of the leaf starch test
cards.b: Boil in water; hot ethanol in a water bath (removes chlorophyll); rinse; add iodine. Blue-black means starch present.

cards.f: Leaf layers from top to bottom
cards.b: Cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll (air spaces), lower epidermis with stomata and guard cells.

cards.f: How are palisade cells adapted for photosynthesis?
cards.b: Tightly packed, many chloroplasts, near the upper surface where most light is absorbed.
Xylem: water and mineral ions, and support. Phloem: sucrose and amino acids.

cards.f: Position of xylem and phloem in a stem and a leaf
cards.b: Stem: bundles in a ring, xylem inside, phloem outside. Leaf: xylem upper side, phloem lower side.

cards.f: Pathway of water through a plant
cards.b: Root hair cells → root cortex cells → xylem → mesophyll cells.

cards.f: Define transpiration, and how does it happen?
cards.b: Loss of water vapour from leaves: water evaporates from mesophyll cells into air spaces, then diffuses out through the stomata.
Movement of sucrose and amino acids in phloem from sources (e.g. leaves) to sinks (e.g. roots, fruits, growing shoots).

short.q: Explain how the structure of a leaf is adapted for photosynthesis. [3]
short.model: The leaf is thin and flat with a large surface area to absorb light and let CO₂ diffuse in quickly; palisade cells contain many chloroplasts; air spaces allow gas diffusion.
points: large surface area to absorb light
thin so short diffusion distance for CO₂
palisade cells with many chloroplasts near upper surface
air spaces / stomata for gas exchange

short.q: A variegated leaf is kept in light and then tested for starch. Describe and explain the result. [2]
short.model: Only the green parts turn blue-black, because only they contain chlorophyll and photosynthesise.
points: green parts blue-black, white parts stay orange-brown

short.q: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis levels off as light intensity increases. [2]
short.model: Another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, becomes limiting, so more light does not increase the rate.

short.q: Explain why a plant wilts on a hot, windy day. [3]
short.model: Water is lost by transpiration faster than roots take it up, so cells lose water and become flaccid, turgor pressure falls and the leaves droop.
points: cells lose water and become flaccid

short.q: State what happens to the rate of transpiration as wind speed increases, and explain why. [2]
short.model: It increases, because the wind blows water vapour away from the leaf, keeping a steeper concentration gradient.
points: water vapour removed, steeper concentration gradient
